summary: Revenue management, service automation, and demand forecasting lead adoption - and AI assistants are becoming a discovery channel hotels now compete inside of. Who tracks it: the sector's research firms, its standards and trade bodies, and the platforms actually running pricing and guest operations.

analysis.body:
According to the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, 8.5% of firms in accommodation and food services reported using AI in the last two weeks, a slight decline from 8.6% in the prior period. This measured figure anchors adoption across a sector spanning hotels, restaurants, and related services. Skift Research indicates that the competitive landscape for hospitality operators has shifted fundamentally, as agentic AI reshapes how travel discovery works and hotel companies must now compete on visibility within AI-compressed recommendation funnels rather than traditional search results alone. HotelWorld AI's Q1 2026 tracking of 2,105+ hotel brands and 131,000 properties globally shows that AI assistants including ChatGPT, Google AI, Perplexity, and Claude now surface hotel recommendations as shortlists rather than link lists, making appearance in AI-generated answers a tracked competitive battleground where only a minority of properties achieve consistent visibility.

Hotel operations deploy AI primarily through property management and revenue optimization platforms. Canary, one of the major hospitality management systems trusted by 20,000+ hotels worldwide, natively integrates with property management systems and CRMs to improve guest experience, streamline operations, and boost revenue. Duetto and SevenRooms operate deeper into guest-experience prediction and revenue management, embedding AI into the operational backbone where daily pricing and service decisions occur. These platforms work from back-office automation through guest-facing services, meaning AI is already embedded in how reservations flow, pricing adapts, and guest communications are routed across major hotel chains.

The restaurant and quick-service sector shows parallel but distinct deployment patterns. The National Restaurant Association tracks food-service automation across chains, where voice AI at the drive-thru and kitchen computer vision systems represent the primary operational focus. Yum Brands deploys voice ordering and kitchen computer vision across its portfolio, while pure-play vendors like SoundHound and ConverseNow power the conversational layer. This concentration of labor-replacement AI in QSR contrasts with the discovery and revenue optimization emphasis in lodging, reflecting structural differences in where margin and operational friction concentrate in each subsector.

The online travel agencies and distribution systems form a second major adoption layer. Expedia Group's marketplace applies generative travel planning and price forecasting to consumer booking experiences, while the global distribution systems that underlie airline and hotel bookings, such as Amadeus and Sabre, apply AI to real-time offer personalization. This means AI visibility and recommendation ranking now matter as much as inventory availability or pricing alone, since travelers increasingly ask AI agents for itineraries rather than browsing ten blue links. Hotels adapting to this shift are building advanced optimizations atop solid search engine optimization to surface in AI-generated answers.

For operators deciding whether to deploy AI, the material suggests three priorities. First, discovery visibility in AI assistants is becoming mandatory competitive infrastructure rather than optional; brands lagging in AI-generated recommendation appearance will lose visibility to travelers who ask rather than scroll. Second, operational AI in revenue management, guest communications, and service routing is concentrated in platforms like Canary that integrate with existing systems, meaning adoption often requires platform migration or deep API work rather than point solutions. Third, the restaurant sector's focus on voice automation and kitchen robotics reflects a labor-availability constraint that lodging has so far addressed differently through revenue management and personalization, so deployment strategy should match the specific labor and margin pressure each operator faces.

https://www.hftp.org/.brief: HFTP, which hosts HITEC, is an international nonprofit association that has been empowering hospitality professionals for “70+ year history” through education, events, networking, research, and skill-building programs. It operates 83 chapters worldwide, including in the United States, Canada, Mexico, Caribbean, UAE, and India. The organization holds a one-day club-professional event each year and a three-day Annual Convention that gathers hundreds of finance and technology professionals for learning, vendor showcases, and networking. HFTP also publishes newsletters such as Hotel Online and Clubs Online, and offers a Corporate Allied Sponsors program to promote companies to its global membership. President James Bina recently shared a letter announcing new resources for members.

https://restaurant.org/.brief: The National Restaurant Association says it helps members build customer loyalty, achieve financial success, and create rewarding careers in foodservice. It offers resources such as a free guide to reduce risk and prepare for public-safety incidents, and a program called “Kids LiveWell” that lets restaurants offer better-for-you meal options to families. The association also publishes a guide titled *Always Ready: Utility Disruptions* to help operators plan for and recover from power, gas, or water outages. It hosts webinars, podcasts, and conferences, including a food-safety webinar with Ecolab experts and a discussion of high-performing beverage categories, and sponsors the Richard E. Marriott Golf Invitational for its Restaurant Advocacy Fund. The site provides the latest news and information aimed at supporting restaurant operations.

https://www.expediagroup.com/.brief: The Expedia Group homepage presents the company as a travel marketplace that connects travelers, partners, and experiences through trusted brands and technology. It says the marketplace offers hotels, vacation rentals, packages, flights, and more, giving travelers many ways to plan and book. The page says, “Expedia Group isn’t just a travel marketplace ,  we’re a catalyst for positive change,” and claims the company aims to create a smarter, more sustainable travel future. It also notes that partners use its B2B technology and advertising solutions to deliver exceptional experiences, and that the company is recognized as a top workplace.
